items.abstract: <jats:p>Purpose: Federated learning (FL) is an established method to preserve privacy of training data in machine learning. Chemical data, often in a pharmaceutical context, have also been used for FL. So far, this has concentrated on per-molecule data. In this paper, we use per-atom data, specifically nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) data, and examine the quality of the results obtained. Furthermore, we study how the number of overall data used for training influences the results. Methods: We use a deep-learning based neural network model to predict NMR shifts. We run this centralized and in a federated learning setting using FedN with random and skewed data distribution. For comparison, we also use a smaller neural network and HOSE codes. Results: We show that with low amounts of data, FL achieved better performance than centralized learning for the smallest datasets considered, and for large amounts of data, is almost as good as centralized learning. On the other 1 hand, we find constantly high variance for FL results, even with the full amount of data available. Conclusion: Federated learning is generally suitable for atom-wise data in chemistry. For low amounts of data, it can even significantly improve results. On the other hand, high variances in results show that there can be negative effects of the use of federated learning as well.</jats:p>
title: Federated Learning for Atom-Wise Chemical Property Prediction: Effects of Dataset Size and Data Heterogeneity in NMR Shift Prediction

items.abstract: Reliable AI-based early warning across courses requires risk probabilities that remain interpretable when learner behavior and outcome prevalence shift. Using the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset, this study develops and evaluates a leakage-controlled cross-module framework that combines temporal behavioral profiling, zero-shot transfer, target-adaptive probability calibration, and capacity-constrained support prioritization. Models were assessed across 28 held-out module-cutoff combinations at days 14, 28, 42, and 56. Earlier presentations supplied learner-disjoint calibration samples covering 10%, 20%, or 30% of the historical target pool, while the chronologically latest presentation was reserved for final evaluation. At the 30% calibration level, the mean Brier score decreased from 0.243 to 0.205, negative log-likelihood from 0.708 to 0.599, expected calibration error from 0.158 to 0.076, and adaptive expected calibration error from 0.161 to 0.078. All seven module-level comparisons favored adaptation for each core metric, with bootstrap intervals excluding zero. Ranking performance was preserved because the selected mappings were predominantly monotonic. Importance weighting and source-side ensemble reweighting did not improve significantly beyond standard target calibration. The results show that modest historical target-domain data can substantially restore probability reliability under cross-course dataset shift and support more interpretable, capacity-aware review.
title: Target-Adaptive Probability Calibration for Reliable Student Risk Prediction under Cross-Module Dataset Shift
